## Proposals to Save the Ringing: From the School to Patronage

The declaration of manual bell ringing as Intangible Cultural Heritage is not a mere protocolary adornment: it entails specific legal obligations for the administrations responsible for the bell towers. In the case of Almuñécar, the City Council and the Diócesis de Granada share the responsibility of preserving a practice that, according to UNESCO files, cannot be limited to preserving the bronzes as museum pieces. A silent bell is, for heritage purposes, a mutilated cultural asset, because its value lies in the human gesture that makes it speak.

The first proposal being considered by the town's veteran bell ringers is the creation of a municipal school for manual bell ringing. This would not be a weekend course or a folkloric workshop, but a stable program with symbolic remuneration for the apprentices, along the lines of the dulzaina or bagpipe schools operating in other communities. The model exists and has yielded results in towns like Villavante, in León, where the annual bell ringers' gathering, held for almost four decades, has served to draw young people with no prior link to the tradition to the ropes with technical curiosity and respect for the inherited codes.

This reference to León is no coincidence. Bell ringers' gatherings function as spaces for oral transmission where the ringing is not learned from sheet music, but by imitating the gesture, listening to the rhythm, and correcting the wrist. Almuñécar could host an Andalusian gathering for manual bell ringing, taking advantage of the network of bell towers on the Granada coast and the presence of deeply rooted brotherhoods. Organizing such an event requires little more than political will, coordination with the parishes, and a modest budget for allowances and promotion.

The local brotherhoods, for their part, represent the strongest link between manual bell ringing and daily life. Subsidizing the training of bell ringers within the brotherhoods would not be an aid to religiosity, but an investment in intangible heritage perfectly justifiable under the Historical Heritage Law. An agreement between the City Council and the brotherhoods could fund learning grants, civil liability insurance for the bell ringers, and the maintenance of access to the towers, which in many cases are currently closed for safety reasons.

Private patronage offers another complementary avenue. Local companies in the tourism and agri-food sectors, which benefit from the image of Almuñécar as a destination with identity, could sponsor specific campaigns or annual ringing cycles. This formula is already applied in the restoration of historical organs and in the financing of early music festivals, with tax deductions that make the contribution attractive. A restored and sounding bell tower is a tangible tourist draw: the visitor not only sees the tower, but hears a language that exists nowhere else in the world.

The Universidad de Granada appears on this map as a little-explored strategic ally. The Department of Social Anthropology and the Department of Art History could collaborate in the systematic documentation of the local ringing, professionally recording the peals, tolls, and clamors that are still preserved in the memory of the active bell ringers. This digitization would not be a mere passive archive: it would serve as teaching material for the municipal school and as a basis for future research on the local variant of the Andalusian bell ringing language.

Digitization, however, cannot replace in-person learning. The bell ringers insist that the ringing is transmitted from hand to hand, with the rope in the palm and the ear attentive to the sway of the bronze. Recordings serve to fix the memory, but not to train bell ringers. That is why the municipal school should combine practical sessions in the tower with the study of sound archives, in a methodology already being tested in Catalonia, where the Generalitat has been funding the training of bell ringers for years in collaboration with the bishoprics.

The economic cost of these measures is low compared to other cultural budgets. Maintaining a bell ringing school with two teachers and a dozen students would not exceed the budget of a fair concert. The restoration of the yokes and clappers of the three main parishes could be financed through the 1.5% cultural levy that the law reserves for heritage conservation. What is lacking is not money, but the decision to consider manual bell ringing as a first-need public cultural service.

Time is running out. Every year that passes without generational renewal, nuances of the local repertoire are lost that no recording will ever fully recover. The local bell ringers who are now over seventy hold in their memory specific ringings for storms, for fires, for calling the council, or for bidding farewell to the dead. In Almuñécar, two ringings announced the death of a woman and three the death of a man, a code that is not universal and varies from town to town. When they are gone, that vocabulary will disappear with the same irreversibility as a language dying out without speakers.

The UNESCO heritage declaration is not a goal, but a starting point. It obliges administrations to protect, but also to promote and transmit. In Almuñécar, protection means opening the towers, paying the master bell ringers, involving the brotherhoods, and convincing young people that learning to ring the bells is not a trade of the past, but a form of belonging to the present. Without concrete measures such as the municipal school, agreements with the brotherhoods, or the university documentation of the ringings, the last manual toll in Almuñécar will not be a metaphor: it will be a specific date on the calendar, a sound that is extinguished forever, and a silence that no automatic bell will ever fill.
